about: English meaning written for this library (en-scriptures): one to three plain sentences per mantra, faithful to the words, following the traditional reading (Śaṅkara). [meaning, [footnotes]]

1.1.1: Om. May Mitra be a blessing to us, may Varuṇa be a blessing; may Aryaman be a blessing to us.
May Indra and Bṛhaspati be a blessing to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide strides be a blessing to us.
Salutation to Brahman. Salutation to you, O Vāyu. You alone are the visible Brahman.
I shall speak of you alone as the visible Brahman; of you alone as ṛta, the right.
Of you alone as satya, the true. May that Brahman protect me; may it protect the speaker (the teacher).
May it protect me; may it protect the speaker.
1.2.1: Om. We shall explain śīkṣā, the science of pronunciation: the sounds, the accent, the length, the force of utterance,
evenness and the joining of sounds. Thus the chapter on pronunciation has been told.
1.3.1: May fame be ours together, both of us (teacher and student); may the radiance of sacred learning be ours together.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the upaniṣad, the secret teaching, of saṃhitā, the joining of sounds,
with regard to the worlds, the lights, learning, offspring and the body.
These they call the great joinings. Now, with regard to the worlds:
the earth is the prior form (the first sound of the joining), heaven the later form;
space is the junction, air the link. So much with regard to the worlds.
1.3.2: Now, with regard to the lights:
fire is the prior form, the sun the later form, the waters the junction,
lightning the link. So much with regard to the lights. Now, with regard to learning:
the teacher is the prior form, the pupil the later form, knowledge the junction,
teaching the link. So much with regard to learning.
1.3.3: Now, with regard to offspring: the mother is the prior form,
the father the later form, the child the junction, begetting the link.
So much with regard to offspring.
1.3.4: Now, with regard to the body: the lower jaw is the prior form,
and the upper jaw the later form, speech the junction, the tongue the link.
So much with regard to the body. These are the great joinings.
He who knows these great joinings, as they have been explained,
is joined with offspring and cattle,
with the radiance of sacred learning, with food to eat and with the heavenly world.
1.4.1: He who is the foremost of the Vedas and takes every form,
who arose from the Vedas, the immortal:
may that Indra strengthen me with wisdom.
O god, may I be one who holds the immortal.
May my body be able; may my tongue be most sweet.
May I hear much with my ears.
You are the sheath of Brahman, covered by the intellect.
1.4.2: She who brings, who increases, who quickly provides for me clothes and cows
and food and drink at all times: bring me then that prosperity,
rich in woolly flocks, together with cattle. Svāhā.
May brahmacārins, students, come to me. Svāhā.
May students come to me from every side. Svāhā.
May students come forth to me. Svāhā.
May students come with their senses restrained. Svāhā.
May students come with calm minds. Svāhā.
1.4.3: May I be famous among people. Svāhā. May I be better than the wealthy. Svāhā.
O Lord (bhaga), may I enter into you, that very one. Svāhā.
O Lord, may you enter into me. Svāhā.
In you, O Lord, who have a thousand branches, I wash myself clean. Svāhā.
As waters flow down the slope, as the months go into the year, in which the days wear away,
so, O Creator, may students come to me from every side. Svāhā.
You are a refuge near at hand: shine forth to me, come to me wholly.
1.5.1: Bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ: these, as is well known, are the three vyāhṛtis, the sacred utterances.
Of these, Māhācamasya made known that fourth one:
mahaḥ. That is Brahman; that is the self; the other gods are its limbs.
Bhūḥ is this world; bhuvaḥ is the space between;
Mahaḥ is the sun; by the sun indeed all the worlds grow great.
1.5.2: Bhūḥ is fire; bhuvaḥ is air; suvaḥ is the sun;
By the moon indeed all the lights grow great. Bhūḥ is the Ṛc verses;
mahaḥ is Brahman. By Brahman indeed all the Vedas grow great.
1.5.3: Bhūḥ is the in-breath (prāṇa); bhuvaḥ is the out-breath (apāna); suvaḥ is the diffused breath (vyāna);
mahaḥ is food. By food indeed all the breaths grow great.
These four are fourfold: the vyāhṛtis are four and four.
knows Brahman. All the gods bring offerings to him.
1.6.1: This space that is within the heart:
in it is this person, made of mind, immortal and golden.
Between the palates, where this hangs down like a teat, is the way to Indra (Brahman);
it goes to where the roots of the hair part, and passes out, splitting the skull.
1.6.2: He is established in fire as bhūḥ, in air as bhuvaḥ,
in the sun as suvaḥ, in Brahman as mahaḥ. He attains self-rule;
he attains the lord of the mind; he becomes lord of speech, lord of sight,
lord of hearing, lord of understanding. Beyond that, he becomes this:
whose self is the true, whose delight is in the breaths, whose mind is bliss,
Meditate on it thus, O Prācīnayogya.
1.7.1: The earth, the space between, heaven, the quarters and the quarters between them;
fire and air, the sun, the moon and the stars;
waters, plants, trees, space and the self. So much with regard to beings.
Now, with regard to the body: the breaths prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, udāna and samāna;
the eye, the ear, the mind, speech and the skin;
skin, flesh, sinew, bone and marrow.
Having set all this out so, the seer said:
By the fivefold one fills out the fivefold.
1.8.1: Om is Brahman. Om is all this.
Om is the word of assent, as is well known; and when told O śrāvaya, they give the response.
With Om they sing the Sāman chants; with Om śom they recite the śastras, the hymns of praise.
With Om the adhvaryu priest gives his response.
With Om the Brahmā priest gives his consent; with Om one gives leave for the agnihotra, the fire offering.
A brāhmaṇa about to recite says Om, thinking: May I attain Brahman;
1.9.1: The right, together with study and teaching.
Truth, together with study and teaching.
Austerity, together with study and teaching.
Control of the senses, together with study and teaching.
Calm of mind, together with study and teaching.
The sacred fires, together with study and teaching.
The agnihotra, together with study and teaching.
Guests, together with study and teaching.
Human dealings, together with study and teaching.
Offspring, together with study and teaching.
Begetting, together with study and teaching.
The birth of grandchildren, together with study and teaching.
Truth alone, says Rāthītara, whose word is truth (Satyavacas).
Austerity alone, says Pauruśiṣṭi, ever given to austerity (Taponitya).
Study and teaching alone, says Nāka Maudgalya;
for that is austerity, that is austerity.
1.10.1: I am the mover of the tree (of worldly existence). My fame is high as a mountain peak.
My pure source is on high; as the immortal is in the sun, rich in food, so I am the pure immortal.
I am wealth, bright with radiance; I am wise, immortal and undecaying.
Such is Triśaṅku's declaration after attaining knowledge.
1.11.1: Having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the pupil:
Speak the truth. Practise dharma, right conduct. Do not neglect your study.
Having brought the teacher the wealth he values, do not cut off the line of your offspring.
Never be careless about truth. Never be careless about dharma.
Never be careless about your welfare. Never be careless about the works that bring prosperity.
Never be careless about study and teaching.
1.11.2: Never be careless about the rites due to the gods and the ancestors. Let your mother be a god to you.
Let your father be a god to you. Let your teacher be a god to you. Let your guest be a god to you.
Whatever deeds are blameless, those should be practised, not others.
Whatever in our conduct is good, that you should follow, not the rest.
1.11.3: Whatever brāhmaṇas there are who are better than we are,
you should give them a seat and let them rest. Give with faith.
Do not give without faith. Give out of your plenty. Give with modesty.
Give with fear. Give with friendliness.
1.11.4: Then, if you have any doubt about a rite, or any doubt about conduct,
whatever brāhmaṇas there are, of sound judgement, devoted to their work, not led by others,
not harsh, and lovers of dharma: as they would act there,
so should you act there. Now, with regard to those who are accused:
whatever brāhmaṇas there are, of sound judgement, devoted to their work, not led by others,
not harsh, and lovers of dharma: as they would act towards them,
so should you act towards them. This is the injunction. This is the counsel.
This is the upaniṣad, the secret teaching, of the Veda. This is the instruction. Thus should one live.
Thus indeed should this be lived.
1.12.1: May Mitra be a blessing to us, may Varuṇa be a blessing; may Aryaman be a blessing to us.
May Indra and Bṛhaspati be a blessing to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide strides be a blessing to us.
Salutation to Brahman. Salutation to you, O Vāyu. You alone are the visible Brahman.
I have spoken of you alone as the visible Brahman; of you alone as ṛta, the right.
Of you alone as satya, the true. That Brahman has protected me; it has protected the speaker.
It has protected me; it has protected the speaker.
iti.1: Here ends the Śīkṣā Vallī of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.
shanti.2: Om. May he (Brahman) protect us both (teacher and student) together. May he nourish us both together. May we both gain strength together.
May what we both have studied be full of light. May we never hate each other.
2.1.1: Om. The knower of Brahman attains the highest. On this, this verse has been declared:
Brahman is truth, knowledge, the infinite.
He who knows it set in the cave, in the highest space,
enjoys all desires at once, as Brahman, the all-knowing.
From this, the Self, space came into being; from space, air;
from air came fire; from fire, the waters; from the waters, the earth;
from the earth, plants; from plants, food; from food, the person.
This person is made of the essence of food. This is its head;
this the right side; this the left side;
this the trunk (ātman); this the tail and support.
On this there is also this verse:
2.2.1: From food indeed creatures are born, whichever rest upon the earth.
Then by food alone they live, and into it they pass in the end.
For food is the eldest of beings; therefore it is called the remedy for all.
They indeed obtain all food who worship food as Brahman.
For food is the eldest of beings; therefore it is called the remedy for all.
From food beings are born; once born, by food they grow.
It is eaten, and it eats beings; therefore it is called food.
Other than this, which is made of the essence of food, there is a self within, made of breath (prāṇa).
By it this one is filled. It too has the shape of a person.
Following the former's human shape, this one too has the shape of a person.
Of it, the in-breath is the head, the diffused breath the right side,
the out-breath the left side, space the trunk,
the earth the tail and support. On this there is also this verse:
2.3.1: The gods breathe after the breath, and so do men and beasts.
For breath is the life of beings; therefore it is called the life of all.
They reach the full span of life who worship breath as Brahman.
For breath is the life of beings; therefore it is called the life of all.
This same is the embodied self of that, the former one.
Other than this, which is made of breath, there is a self within, made of mind.
By it this one is filled. It too has the shape of a person.
Following the former's human shape, this one too has the shape of a person.
Of it, the Yajus is the head, the Ṛc the right side, the Sāman the left side,
the teaching (ādeśa, the Brāhmaṇa) the trunk, the hymns of Atharvan and Aṅgiras the tail and support.
On this there is also this verse:
2.4.1: From which words turn back, together with the mind, without reaching it:
knowing that bliss of Brahman, one never fears.
This same is the embodied self of that, the former one.
Other than this, which is made of mind, there is a self within, made of understanding (vijñāna).
By it this one is filled. It too has the shape of a person.
Following the former's human shape, this one too has the shape of a person. Of it, faith is the head,
what is right (ṛta) the right side,
truth the left side, yoga the trunk, mahaḥ the tail and support.
On this there is also this verse:
2.5.1: Understanding performs the sacrifice, and it performs works as well.
All the gods worship understanding as Brahman, the eldest. If one knows understanding as Brahman,
and if he does not stray from it, he leaves his sins in the body
and attains all desires. This same is the embodied self of that,
the former one. Other than this, which is made of understanding,
there is a self within, made of bliss (ānanda). By it this one is filled.
It too has the shape of a person.
Following the former's human shape, this one too has the shape of a person. Of it, joy is the head,
great delight the left side, bliss the trunk, Brahman the tail and support.
On this there is also this verse:
2.6.1: He becomes as good as non-existent, if he knows Brahman as non-existent.
If he knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as existing.
This same is the embodied self of that, the former one.
Now, therefore, the questions that follow.
Does anyone who does not know go to that world on departing?
Or does anyone who knows attain that world on departing?
He desired: May I be many, may I be born. He practised austerity.
Having practised austerity, he created all this, whatever there is.
When he had created it, he entered that very thing. Entering it,
he became sat and tyat, the formed and the formless,
what can be defined and what cannot, the supported and the unsupported,
the conscious and the unconscious, the true and the untrue. The True became
all this, whatever there is; that they call the True.
On this there is also this verse:
2.7.1: In the beginning all this was non-being; from that, being was born.
That made its own self; that is why it is called sukṛta, the self-made.
That which is the self-made is indeed the essence (rasa).
For only on gaining the essence does one become blissful. Who would breathe out, who
would breathe in, if this bliss were not there in space (the cave of the heart)?
It is this alone that gives bliss.
For when one finds, in this which is unseen, bodiless, beyond words and without support, a fearless
footing, then he has gone to fearlessness.
But when one makes in this even the least difference,
then there is fear for him. That itself is fear to the knower who does not reflect (on oneness).
On this there is also this verse:
2.8.1: From fear of it the wind blows; from fear the sun rises.
From fear of it fire and Indra run, and Death, the fifth.
This is the inquiry into bliss:
let there be a young man, a good young man, learned,
most able to command, most firm, most strong;
and let this whole earth, full of wealth, be his:
that is one unit of human bliss. A hundred units of human bliss
2.8.2: make one unit of the bliss of the human gandharvas. So too is the bliss of one versed in the Veda and untouched by desire.
A hundred units of the bliss of the human gandharvas
make one unit of the bliss of the divine gandharvas. So too is the bliss of one versed in the Veda and untouched by desire.
A hundred units of the bliss of the divine gandharvas
make one unit of the bliss of the ancestors, whose world lasts long.
So too is the bliss of one versed in the Veda and untouched by desire.
A hundred units of the bliss of the ancestors, whose world lasts long,
make one unit of the bliss of the gods born in the world of the gods (ājānaja).
2.8.3: So too is the bliss of one versed in the Veda and untouched by desire.
A hundred units of the bliss of the gods born in the world of the gods
make one unit of the bliss of the gods by works,
who reach the gods by their works. So too is the bliss of one versed in the Veda and untouched by desire.
A hundred units of the bliss of the gods by works
make one unit of the bliss of the gods. So too is the bliss of one versed in the Veda and untouched by desire.
A hundred units of the bliss of the gods make one unit of the bliss of Indra.
2.8.4: So too is the bliss of one versed in the Veda and untouched by desire. A hundred units of the bliss of Indra
make one unit of the bliss of Bṛhaspati. So too is the bliss of one versed in the Veda and untouched by desire.
A hundred units of the bliss of Bṛhaspati make one unit of the bliss of Prajāpati.
So too is the bliss of one versed in the Veda and untouched by desire.
A hundred units of the bliss of Prajāpati
make one unit of the bliss of Brahmā. So too is the bliss of one versed in the Veda and untouched by desire.
2.8.5: He who is here in the person, and he who is there in the sun: he is one.
He who knows this, turning away from this world,
reaches this self made of food,
reaches this self made of breath,
reaches this self made of mind,
reaches this self made of understanding,
reaches this self made of bliss.
On this there is also this verse:
2.9.1: From which words turn back, together with the mind, without reaching it:
Him indeed this does not torment:
Why did I not do the good? Why did I do evil?
He who knows this treats both of these as the Self and strengthens himself;
for he treats both of these as the Self and strengthens himself, he who knows this.
This is the upaniṣad, the secret teaching.
iti.2: Here ends the Brahmānanda Vallī of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.
shanti.3: Om. May he (Brahman) protect us both (teacher and student) together. May he nourish us both together. May we both gain strength together.
May what we both have studied be full of light. May we never hate each other.
3.1.1: Bhṛgu, the well-known son of Varuṇa, went to his father Varuṇa and said:
Venerable one, teach me Brahman. Varuṇa told him this:
Food, breath, the eye, the ear, the mind and speech.
Then he said to him: That from which these beings are born,
by which, once born, they live,
and to which they go at the end and into which they enter and merge — seek to know that: that is Brahman.
He practised austerity. Having practised austerity, he …
3.2.1: He knew that food is Brahman.
For truly it is from food that these beings are born; once born, they live by food;
and at the end they go to food and enter and merge into it. Having known this,
he went once more to his father Varuṇa and said:
Venerable one, teach me Brahman. Varuṇa said to him:
Seek to know Brahman by austerity; austerity is Brahman.
He practised austerity. Having practised austerity, he …
3.3.1: He knew that breath is Brahman.
For truly it is from breath that these beings are born; once born, they live by breath;
and at the end they go to breath and enter and merge into it. Having known this,
he went once more to his father Varuṇa and said:
Venerable one, teach me Brahman. Varuṇa said to him:
Seek to know Brahman by austerity; austerity is Brahman.
He practised austerity. Having practised austerity, he …
3.4.1: He knew that the mind is Brahman.
For truly it is from the mind that these beings are born; once born, they live by the mind;
and at the end they go to the mind and enter and merge into it. Having known this,
he went once more to his father Varuṇa and said:
Venerable one, teach me Brahman. Varuṇa said to him:
Seek to know Brahman by austerity; austerity is Brahman.
He practised austerity. Having practised austerity, he …
3.5.1: He knew that understanding is Brahman.
For truly it is from understanding that these beings are born; once born, they live by understanding;
and at the end they go to understanding and enter and merge into it. Having known this,
he went once more to his father Varuṇa and said:
Venerable one, teach me Brahman. Varuṇa said to him:
Seek to know Brahman by austerity; austerity is Brahman.
He practised austerity. Having practised austerity, he …
3.6.1: He knew that bliss is Brahman.
For truly it is from bliss that these beings are born; once born, they live by bliss;
and at the end they go to bliss and enter and merge into it.
This is the knowledge known by Bhṛgu and taught by Varuṇa; it is established in the highest space.
He who knows this becomes established. He becomes rich in food and an eater of food.
He becomes great in offspring, in cattle and in the radiance of sacred learning,
3.7.1: Let one not speak ill of food: that is the vow. Breath, truly, is food,
and the body is its eater. The body is established in breath;
breath is established in the body. So this food is established in food.
He who knows this food thus established in food becomes established.
He becomes rich in food and an eater of food. He becomes great in offspring,
in cattle and in the radiance of sacred learning, and great in fame.
3.8.1: Let one not reject food: that is the vow. Water, truly, is food,
and light is its eater. Light is established in water;
water is established in light. So this food is established in food.
He who knows this food thus established in food becomes established.
He becomes rich in food and an eater of food. He becomes great in offspring,
in cattle and in the radiance of sacred learning, and great in fame.
3.9.1: Let one make food plentiful: that is the vow. The earth, truly, is food,
and space is its eater. Space is established in the earth;
the earth is established in space.
So this food is established in food.
He who knows this food thus established in food becomes established.
He becomes rich in food and an eater of food. He becomes great in offspring,
in cattle and in the radiance of sacred learning, and great in fame.
3.10.1: Let one turn away no one who comes for lodging: that is the vow.
Therefore let one gain much food by whatever means.
Those who have food tell such a guest that food is ready for him.
Food made ready and given in the foremost way, with honour —
for the giver food is made ready in the foremost way.
Food made ready and given in the middling way —
for him food is made ready in the middling way.
Food made ready and given in the lowest way, with disregard —
for him food is made ready in the lowest way.
3.10.2: He who knows this. Let one meditate on Brahman in speech as keeping (what one has); in the in-breath and the out-breath as gaining and keeping;
in the hands as action; in the feet as movement; in the organ of excretion as release.
These are the meditations within man. Now those among the gods: in rain as satisfaction;
3.10.3: in cattle as fame; in the stars as light;
in the organ of generation as procreation, immortality and joy; in space as all.
Let one meditate on that as the support: he comes to have a firm support.
Let one meditate on it as greatness: he becomes great. Let one meditate on it as mind:
3.10.4: Let one meditate on it as homage: the things he desires bow down to him.
Let one meditate on it as Brahman: he comes to possess Brahman.
Let one meditate on it as the parimara of Brahman, that in which the gods die away:
around him die the rivals who hate him,
and around him die the rivals who are not dear to him.
He who is here in the person, and he who is there in the sun: he is one.
3.10.5: He who knows this, turning away from this world,
having reached this self made of food,
having reached this self made of breath,
having reached this self made of mind,
having reached this self made of understanding,
having reached this self made of bliss,
roams these worlds, eating as he wills, taking what form he wills,
and abides singing this sāman, the chant: Hāvu! Hāvu! Hāvu!
3.10.6: I am food, I am food, I am food.
I am the one who eats food, I am the one who eats food, I am the one who eats food.
I am the one who joins them, I am the one who joins, I am the one who joins.
I am the first-born of ṛta, the true,
born before the gods, the navel (the centre) of immortality.
He who gives me away, he it is who keeps me so.
I, food, eat the one who eats food.
I have overcome the whole world.
My light is like the sun.
He who knows this. This is the upaniṣad, the secret teaching.
iti.3: Here ends the Bhṛgu Vallī of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.

1.1.1: Śaṅkara takes Mitra, Varuṇa and the rest as the gods of the body: of the in-breath and the day, the out-breath and the night, the eye and the sun, strength, speech and intellect, and the feet; and Brahman here as Vāyu, on whom the fruit of all action depends.
Ṛtaṃ vadiṣyāmi, satyaṃ vadiṣyāmi is also read: I shall speak what is right, I shall speak the truth.
1.3.1: Śaṅkara takes the opening prayer as the pupil's, and this upaniṣad as a meditation: one is to see the earth in the first sound of a joining, heaven in the second, and so on.
1.3.4: Śaṅkara takes knows here as meditates on.
1.4.1: Śaṅkara takes this anuvāka as a prayer to Om: mantras muttered by one who seeks wisdom, and offered with svāhā as oblations by one who seeks prosperity; Indra is the Lord of all desires, the immortal is the knowledge of Brahman, and Om is the sheath of Brahman because Brahman is found in it, hidden from ordinary understanding.
1.4.3: Śaṅkara takes entering as becoming one with the Lord, who is Om here, and the washing as cleansing oneself of sinful deeds.
1.5.2: Śaṅkara takes Brahman here as Om, since the subject is words.
1.6.1: Śaṅkara takes this way as the suṣumṇā channel, which rises from the heart and leaves the head at the crown; by it the knower of the self made of mind departs.
1.7.1: Śaṅkara takes the self in the first list as Virāṭ, the cosmic person; and the last words as: by the fivefold within the body one fills out the fivefold without, knowing them as one. The sacrifice too is fivefold (pāṅkta).
1.8.1: Śaṅkara takes Brahman in the last lines as the Veda, which the brāhmaṇa about to study hopes to master, or as the supreme Self.
1.10.1: Śaṅkara takes these as the words of the seer Triśaṅku, who had realised Brahman, declaring like Vāmadeva that his work was done; they are recited to give rise to knowledge. The pure source is the supreme Brahman; amṛtokṣitaḥ is also read as sprinkled with the immortal.
1.11.3: Śaṅkara also reads: in their assembly you should not so much as breathe, but only take in the substance of what they say.
shanti.2: Śaṅkara says this śānti pāṭha, recited with Śaṃ no mitraḥ at the opening of the Brahmānanda Vallī, quiets the obstacles to the knowledge of Brahman about to be taught.
2.1.1: Śaṅkara takes the cave as the intellect, set in the space of the heart, and saha brahmaṇā vipaścitā as one with Brahman, the all-knowing; it is also read as together with Brahman, the all-knowing.
2.2.1: Śaṅkara takes space here as samāna, the breath in the middle of the body, and the earth as its deity, who holds the breath in place.
2.3.1: Śaṅkara takes this same is the embodied self of that, the former one as: the self just described (made of breath) is the self within the body of the one before it (made of food); so too in the sheaths that follow. The gods are Agni and the rest, or the senses.
2.4.1: Śaṅkara takes understanding as the intellect that settles the meaning of the Veda, yoga as composure of mind, and mahaḥ as mahat, the great principle, the first-born.
2.5.1: Śaṅkara takes the self made of bliss as still an effect, a sheath, not Brahman itself; Brahman, truth, knowledge, the infinite, innermost and the support of all, is its tail. Joy is the pleasure of seeing what is dear, delight the gladness of gaining it, great delight that gladness heightened.
2.6.1: Śaṅkara takes that world as the supreme Self; austerity (tapas) as knowledge, the reflection before creation; and the first true as the true of everyday dealings, while the True that became all this is Brahman, the ultimately true.
2.7.1: Śaṅkara takes non-being as Brahman unmanifest, before name and form, not sheer nothing; and he reads udaram antaram as ut aram antaram, even the least difference.
2.8.1: Āśiṣṭha means literally the quickest; Śaṅkara takes it as āśāstṛtama, the most able to command.
2.8.2: Śaṅkara takes the human gandharvas as men who became gandharvas through works and knowledge, and the ājānaja gods as those born in the world of the gods through rites taught in the smṛti.
2.8.3: Śaṅkara takes the gods by works as those who reach the gods by Vedic rites alone, such as the agnihotra.
2.8.4: Śaṅkara takes Brahmā as Hiraṇyagarbha, in whom all these grades of bliss become one; even this is only a fraction of the supreme bliss.
2.8.5: Śaṅkara takes turning away from this world as turning back from all objects, seen and unseen, wanting none (pretya commonly means after death); and reaching each self as knowing it in turn and passing beyond it, not going anywhere.
2.9.1: Śaṅkara says the knower sees both the good and the evil as the supreme Self, so neither torments him.
3.1.1: Śaṅkara takes these as the doors to knowing Brahman: food is the body, breath the eater within it, and the eye, ear, mind and speech the means of perceiving.
Śaṅkara takes tapas, austerity, here as the stilling and one-pointedness of the senses and the mind.
3.2.1: Śaṅkara takes the repeated teaching of austerity to show that, until the search comes to rest, austerity is the foremost means of knowing Brahman.
3.6.1: For Śaṅkara the highest space is the cave of the space within the heart, the supreme non-dual bliss; he who knows thus is established in that bliss, the supreme Brahman, and becomes Brahman.
3.10.1: Śaṅkara also takes mukhataḥ, madhyataḥ and antataḥ as the first, middle and last part of life: food comes back to the giver as and when he gave it.
3.10.4: For Śaṅkara the parimara is the air, in which the five deities, lightning, rain, the moon, the sun and fire, die away; the air is one with space, so space is meditated on as the parimara of Brahman. Elsewhere brahmaṇaḥ parimara also names a rite for the destruction of rivals.
3.10.5: Śaṅkara takes turning away from this world as turning back from all objects, seen and unseen, wanting none (pretya commonly means after death); and having reached each self as knowing it in turn and passing beyond it, not going anywhere.
Hāvu is a cry of utmost wonder, meaning aho.
3.10.6: For Śaṅkara the śloka is the union of food and its eater, and the ślokakṛt the conscious one who makes it; the word itself means one who makes a sound, who calls out. He who eats food is the one who eats it without giving to those who ask.
